aztecsalsa.title: Aztec Salsa — Tasting History
aztecsalsa.body:
Watch the Video
The 16th century Franciscan missionary Fray Bernardino de Sahagún wrote about all aspects of Aztec culture, including their food. He mentions many kinds of salsa ranging from mild to hot, and the combination of chiles and tomatoes shows up all over the place.
Aztecs ate salsa with things like tamales, turkey, venison, and seafood. They didn’t have a good source of fat for frying, so tortilla chips didn’t come around until after the Spanish brought over livestock like beef and pork.
While there isn’t an exact recipe for this, using Sahagún’s writings, we can recreate a kind of salsa that wouldn’t have been out of place in an Aztec market. Since the kinds of salsa the Aztecs ate were so varied, feel free to use the kinds of tomatoes and chiles that you like. If you don’t have a high tolerance for heat, I’d recommend not using the orange peppers that I bought because they were pretty (they were habañeros).
“
He sells food, sauce, hot sauces; . . . mild red chile sauce, yellow chile sauce, hot chile sauce . . . sauce of smoked chile . . . sauce of large tomatoes, sauce of ordinary tomatoes . . .
They also ate many kinds of chile stews; one kind . . . was made of chile and tomatoes; another kind was made of yellow chile and tomatoes.
”
— Bernardino de Sahagún, 16th century
aztecsalsa.ing:
Ingredients:
Yellow chiles, I used 3 caribe/güero chiles and 2 habañeros*
1 Anaheim chile
Tomatoes, I used 4 large heirloom tomatoes
A large pinch salt
*I picked the habañeros completely by accident. Feel free to use them if you like very spicy salsa, but you can use any chiles you like for this.
Instructions:
Heat a pan over high heat, then work in batches to give some char to the chiles and tomatoes. Keep an eye on them and turn them so that you get some nice blistering all over. Be careful with the tomatoes, as you don’t want the skin to come off.
Place the charred chiles and tomatoes in a large pot and cover them with water. Bring the pot to a simmer and let them cook for 12 to 15 minutes. After they’ve cooked, take them out of the pot. Now it’s okay if the tomato skins come off. Whether or not you keep them in the salsa is up to you.
Let the chiles and tomatoes cool, then remove the seeds and ribs from the chiles. Chop the chiles and tomatoes. The finer you chop them, the less work you’ll have to do grinding them up.
If you have a new molcajete, check the notes below for instructions on how to season it before you use it. Place the chopped chiles and tomatoes into a molcajete along with the salt, then grind everything together until it’s as smooth as you want it. You can also do this step in a blender or food processor.
For extra authenticity, serve the salsa forth with the tamales from the
Tasting History Cookbook
, turkey, venison, or seafood, but I won’t judge you if you reach for a bag of chips.
Notes
To season a new molcajete before you use it, put some dry rice and a little salt in the molcajete and grind it in so that the rice and salt fills in all the little holes. Rub some garlic or onion over it, then let it dry before using.

baklava.title: Baklava — Tasting History
baklava.body:
Watch the Video
Though there are various theories on the origins of baklava, what’s not up for debate is how it has been a popular dessert throughout a large area, and there have been many varieties depending on place and time. The filling could include nuts, lentils, clotted cream, rose water, cinnamon, and musk, just to name a few. It was given as special gifts, included in large banquets, and written of with much fondness and a dash of hyperbole.
The version I opted to make is simple and delicious. You can make your own phyllo, but that’s not a process I’m eager to repeat, so I buy mine, which makes this a surprisingly easy dish to prepare. The pastry is flaky and crisp, the sweetness level is just right, and the ghee adds a wonderful richness.
“
Ordinary Baklava.
Roll out thin sheets of dough like those for the fine börek described in the fifth chapter. Once the tray has been greased, spread clarified butter after every five sheets. When there are ten sheets, sprinkle on crushed hazelnuts, pistachios, or almonds. When there are fifteen sheets, add butter; when there are twenty, sprinkle on one of the aforementioned nuts. If the pastry sheets are very thin, continue until there are fifty or sixty; if they are somewhat thicker, until there are thirty-five or forty. Cut it into the shape of baklava, then pour hot browned clarified butter over the top with a ladle. When it is baking in the oven, take enough sugar or honey for the size of the tray and boil it with two or three cups of water until it reaches a fairly thick consistency. When the baklava is fully browned in the oven and taken out, slowly pour the sugar syrup or honey over it with a ladle. Then arrange it neatly on plates, sprinkle fine powdered sugar over it, and eat.
”
— Melceü’t-Tabbâhîn by Mehmed Kâmil, 1844
baklava.ing:
Ingredients:
1 cup (235 ml) water
1 cup (200 g) sugar
1 cup (340 g) honey
1 cup (225 g) melted ghee or clarified butter, more or less as needed
4 cups (500 g) pistachios, hazelnuts, or almonds, roughly chopped*
45 sheets phyllo or yufka
*You want a mix of large and small pieces.
Instructions:
Combine the sugar and water in a small saucepan over medium heat. Stir until the sugar is dissolved, then let it come to a simmer. Once it simmers, stir in the honey. Simmer for 10 minutes, then take it off the heat and let it cool to room temperature while you make the rest of the baklava.
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Grease a deep sheet pan or other baking dish with some of the melted ghee. It’s helpful if your dish is the same size as your phyllo sheets, but if it’s not, trim them to match. Lay down 5 sheets of phyllo then gently brush the top sheet with a thin, even layer of ghee. You don’t want the dough to tear, so be careful.
Lay down 5 more sheets of phyllo, then brush the top one with a thin, even layer of the ghee. Sprinkle about 1/4 of the nuts evenly over it, making sure they get to the edges.
Lay down 5 more sheets of phyllo, then brush the top one with a thin, even layer of ghee.
Once again, lay down 5 more sheets of phyllo, then brush the top one with a thin, even layer of ghee. Sprinkle another 1/4 of the nuts evenly over this layer, making sure they get to the edges.
Repeat the process of 5 sheets of phyllo, melted ghee, 5 sheets of phyllo, melted ghee and 1/4 of the nuts until you have a total of 4 layers of nuts and 40 sheets of phyllo.
Now lay down 4 sheets of phyllo and brush the top with a thin, even layer of ghee. Place the last sheet of phyllo on top, then brush that with a thin, even layer of ghee. You can also brush ghee in between all 5 of these sheets of phyllo if you’d like.
Cut the baklava into whatever shapes you like; I did diamonds. Spoon more of the melted ghee over the cut baklava, making sure that it gets down into the cuts and is sprea

brationapplesauce.title: B Ration Apple Cranberry Sauce — Tasting History
brationapplesauce.body:
Watch the Video
The A Ration (fresh foods) and B Ration (dehydrated, canned, or otherwise preserved foods) made up 79% of the US soldier’s diet in World War II. While dehydrated and powdered foods aren’t the ideal, sometimes they can turn out to be rather tasty, like this apple cranberry sauce.
First off, this is more of a compote than a sauce, but other than that, I don’t have any complaints. It tastes (not surprisingly) like applesauce with some cranberries tossed in, and would be even better with a bit of nutmeg or cinnamon, which they would have had in the field kitchens.
“
NO. 893. APPLE CRANBERRY SAUCE
Yield: 100 3-ounce servings or 1 1/2 serving spoons each.
Apple nuggets, dehydrated…2 1/4 pounds (3 No. 56 dippers)
Water (for apples)...6 1/2 quarts (6 1/2 No. 56 dippers)
Cranberries, dehydrated, whole, or Cranberries, dehydrated, sliced* 1/2 pound (1/3 No. 56 dipper)
Water…2 1/2 quarts (2 1/2 No. 56 dippers)
Sugar, granulated…5 pounds (2 1/2 No. 56 dippers)
*If compressed cranberry slices are used, do not use volume measurements. Note weight given on box.
1. Soak apples in water 20 to 40 minutes
2. Add cranberries and water to apple nuggets.
3. Bring to a boil over a slow fire and simmer 15 minutes. Add sugar and continue boiling for 5 minutes. Cool and serve.
”
— TM 10-412 US Army Technical Manual. Army Recipes by the U.S. War Department, 1946
brationapplesauce.ing:
Ingredients:
1 3/4 cups (110 g) dehydrated apple nuggets*
3 1/2 cups (835 ml) water
1/4 cup (25 g) dried cranberries
1 heaping cup (225 g) sugar
*See Notes below.
Instructions:
Combine the apple nuggets and 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) water in a medium pot and let the apple rehydrate for 30 minutes.
After the apple has rehydrated, stir in the cranberries and the remaining 1 cup (235 ml) water.
Set the pot over medium-high heat and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 15 minutes.
Stir in the sugar and cook for another 5 minutes.
Let it cool and serve it forth with
Vienna Sausage and Beans
and
Pineapple Milk
for a complete B Ration meal.
Notes
Link to dehydrated apple nuggets:
https://amzn.to/3Yopn24

kvass.title: Kvass — Tasting History
kvass.body:
Watch the Video
Kvass has been made in Eastern Europe for hundreds of years. It can be made with things like flour, beets (like for borscht), and bread. This recipe from 16th century Russia uses bread without any additional yeast. It’s pretty bare bones when it comes to instructions, so I used other recipes from the 18th and 19th centuries to fill in the gaps.
I was pleasantly surprised with how much I liked this. I used dark rye bread and didn’t add the optional brewer’s yeast or raisins, and I ended up with a lightly effervescent kvass that tasted like I was drinking that loaf of good dark rye bread with a wonderful sweetness. I highly recommend making it; it’s easy, only requires a few ingredients, and is absolutely delicious.
“
Ordinary kvass.
To brew ordinary kvass, take four parts honey and strain it until clear. Put it in a jar and ferment it using an ordinary soft loaf, without additional yeast. When it is done, pour it into a cask.
”
— Domostroi, 16th century
kvass.ing:
Ingredients:
3 quarts (3 L) water
1 lb (450 g) dark rye bread*
2/3 cup (225 g) raw honey*
A pinch of brewer’s yeast**, optional
A handful of raisins**, optional
*See Notes below.
**These weren’t included in the 16th century recipe, but occur in 18th and 19th century recipes and ensure a smoother fermenting process and add flavor.
Instructions:
This step is optional, but brings out a little more flavor. Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Tear the bread into small pieces and arrange them in a single layer on a baking sheet. Bake for about 5 to 10 minutes, or until the bread is toasted.
In a large pot, bring the water to a boil. Once it boils, turn the heat off, then add the bread pieces. Cover the pot and let it soak for at least 2 hours, preferably overnight.
After the bread has soaked, transfer the bread and water to a large sterilized container for fermenting. Stir in the honey. If you’re using the brewer’s yeast and raisins, add them now. Cover the container with some cheesecloth, securing it tightly, or cover with a lid specifically for fermenting with an airlock. Do not cover the container tightly with a regular lid, as the gases from fermenting will make the container explode. Put the container in a warm place.
After a few hours, the bread should have fallen to the bottom. Leave the jar in a warm place for about three days. By the second day, you should start to see some of the bread pieces floating either suspended in the liquid or on top of it. This means that the fermentation process is working and is making little bubbles. The kvass is done fermenting when most of the bread, and the raisins if you’re using them, are floating on the top.
Strain the kvass through several layers of cheesecloth. You won’t get all of the sediment out, but you’ll get the pieces of bread and some of the sediment. I strained mine 3 times. The kvass will be cloudy. A 19th century cookbook suggests saving some of the sediment for fermenting the next batch, then feeding the rest to th

medievalcherrycheesecake.title: Medieval Cherry Cheesecake — Tasting History
medievalcherrycheesecake.body:
Watch the Video
If you were in medieval Europe and wanted to make this torte, you would need to visit separate merchants for the grain, dairy products, cherries, sugar, and spices, and this was assuming that you were there on the right day when all of those merchants would be present. It would be worth the effort, though.
This cheesecake-like torte is fantastic. The cherries come through strongly with the barest hint of rose, and the spices are well balanced. The parmesan doesn’t do a whole lot except maybe add some salt, so you’d probably be fine if you left it out and added in a bit of salt instead. Definitely recommend!
“
Take the darkest cherries you can find, remove their stones, and grind them very well in a mortar, and take red roses chopped very finely with a knife, and a little fresh cheese and a little good aged cheese, adding spices, that is cinnamon, ginger, and a little pepper and some sugar; and you mix all these very well, adding to them also three or four eggs according to the quantity that you wish to make, and with the crust underneath, put it to cook gently in the pan. And when it is cooked, you sprinkle it with some sugar and rosewater.
”
— Libro de arte coquinaria by Maestro Martino da Como, 15th century
medievalcherrycheesecake.ing:
Ingredients:
Crust
1 cup (226 g) salted butter, diced
3 cups (360 g) flour
1/2 cup (120 ml) very cold water
Filling
1 1/2 lbs (680 g) cherries, the darkest you can find, or 1 lb (450 g) pitted cherries
3 eggs
1 1/2 cups (375 g) fresh cheese, I used ricotta
1 cup (200 g) sugar
1 1/2 teaspoons ginger
1 1/2 teaspoons cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon black pepper
2 tablespoons aged cheese, I used parmesan
A handful fragrant edible rose petals, red if you can find them, or 1 teaspoon rose water
Rose water, for topping
Powdered sugar, for topping
Cherries, for decoration, optional
Fresh edible roses, for decoration, optional
Instructions:
For the crust:
In a large bowl, rub the butter into the flour until it has the texture of bread crumbs. Sprinkle about 1 teaspoon of the water over the flour mixture and work it in. Add more water only if you need to, 1 teaspoon at a time just until the dough comes together.
Turn the dough out onto a work surface and knead it a few times until it’s smooth enough to form a disc. If the dough isn’t holding together or has a lot of cracks, add a bit more water.
Wrap the disc of dough and let it rest in the fridge for 30 minutes.
Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
If you’re using a tin with a removable bottom, cut out a piece of parchment paper to fit the bottom and place the parchment on it. If you’re using a regular pie dish, skip this step.
After the dough has rested, roll it out into circle large enough to line your baking vessel and transfer the dough into it. If the dough tears, you can patch it with some scraps.
Line the dough with foil or parchment and fill it with baking beans. Bake for 15 minutes, then carefully remove the foil and baking beans and return the crust to the oven for another 10 minutes, or until it’s fully cooked.
Let the crust cool completely before adding the filling.
For the filling:
Reduce the oven temperature to 325°F (165°C).
Pit the cherries, and I recommend wearing gloves unless you don’t mind staining your hands with ch

medievalmustard.title: Medieval Mustard — Tasting History
medievalmustard.body:
Watch the Video
One of the ways of preparing early medieval French mustard included grinding the seeds with grape must (the seeds, skins, and juice of unfermented wine grapes). In medieval Latin, this was called
mustum ardens
, or “burning must.” Later, this became moustarde/moutarde, and mustard was a flavoring for both the common people, as it could be grown at home, and for the wealthy, as seen as part of lavish feasts.
This recipe, from much later in the Middle Ages, doesn’t contain must, but it is delicious. It has some kick to it, much more than the
Roman mustard
made with honey, and would be excellent with some meat or even on a hotdog. You can still buy the version made with must, just look for
moutarde violette.
“
Moustarde . . . If you want to make it good and at leisure, put the mustard seed to soak overnight in good vinegar; then have it ground well in the mill, and little by little thin it with vinegar. And if you have any spices left over from making jelly, clare, hippocras, or sauces, have them ground with it, and afterward let it rest.
”
— Le Viandier de Taillevent by Guillaume Tirel, c. 1300
medievalmustard.ing:
Ingredients:
1/4 cup (50 g) white mustard seeds*, or any other color you like
About 1/4 cup (60 ml) wine vinegar, white or red
2 tablespoons sugar
1 teaspoon cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon ginger
1/2 teaspoon nutmeg
1/2 teaspoon mace
1/8 teaspoon cloves
2 cups (475 ml) wine, white or red
*White mustard seeds and yellow mustard seeds are the same thing.
Instructions:
Place the mustard seeds in a small bowl, pour enough vinegar over them to cover them (you may need more or less than 1/4 cup), and let them soak overnight.
Make the hippocras by mixing together the sugar, cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, mace, and cloves. Place this mixture on a couple layers of cheesecloth, then gather the cheesecloth up and tie it with some kitchen twine to make a little sachet. Place the sachet in the wine and let it soak overnight.
The next day, grind the soaked mustard seeds in a mortar until it's as smooth as you like.
Mix in some more vinegar a little at a time until you get a nice thick consistency. You can thin it out as much as you like, but the vinegar may start to overpower the flavor.
Take the sachet out of the wine, open it up, and add the spices to the mustard. You can serve the hippocras forth as a drink. Stir the spices into the mustard, let it sit for about 10 minutes, then serve it forth.

oldfashioned.title: Old-Fashioned Old Fashioned — Tasting History
oldfashioned.body:
Watch the Video
The word cocktail seems to have emerged in the late 18th century, and back then it wasn’t referring to a whole host of mixed drinks, but to
a
drink. You had a glass of cocktail. The 1806 recipe here comes from a response to a question of what cocktail is, and while it could be made with any kind of spirits, it was specific in including sugar, water, and bitters.
About 30 years later, we get a more specific description that includes a ratio of water to liquor, and the addition of nutmeg, which I found delightful.
By 1895, long enough for people to wish for an “old-fashioned cocktail” rather than the new fangled ones, the old fashioned resembles the modern version, but with a lemon twist instead of orange.
The 1895 version is a lot stronger than the 1806 version, but both are delicious. I was surprised to really enjoy the nutmeg in the 1806 version, and we should definitely be adding it to more cocktails.
“
Cock tail, then is a stimulating liquor, composed of spirits of any kind, sugar, water, and bitters.
”
— Hudson Balance and Columbian Repository, May 13, 1806
“
…a third of the spirit to two-thirds of the water; add bitters, and enrich with sugar and nutmeg.
”
— Transatlantic Sketches by Captain James Edward Alexander, 1833
“
Dissolve a small lump of sugar with a little water in a whiskey-glass; add two dashes Angostura bitters, a small piece ice, a piece lemon-peel, one jigger whiskey. Mix with a small bar-spoon and serve, leaving spoon in the glass.
”
— Modern American Drinks by George J. Kappeler, 1895
oldfashioned.ing:
Ingredients:
1806 Version
1 sugar cube
Several drops of bitters*
2 ounces liquor*
3 ounces water
Nutmeg
1895 Version
1 sugar cube
1 oz water
2 dashes Angostura bitters
1 ice cube, about the size of a small egg
1 strip lemon peel
1.5 ounces whiskey, I used rye
*See Notes below.
Instructions:
For the 1806 version:
Place the sugar cube in a cocktail glass. Back then, this resembled a small wine glass, and it would eventually become the martini glass.
Add the bitters to the sugar cube. You want there to be enough so that all of the sugar absorbs some bitters.
Muddle the bitters-soaked sugar, then add the liquor and water. Stir until the sugar has dissolved (or at least mostly).
Grate a little fresh nutmeg on top, then serve it forth.
For the 1895 version:
Place the sugar cube in a rocks glass. Add the water, then muddle the sugar cube so that it mostly dissolves in the water.
Add the bitters and ice, then twist the lemon peel over the glass and drop it in.
Add the whiskey, give it a stir, and serve it forth with the spoon. For extra authenticity, after you’ve drunk the cocktail, use the spoon to eat any sugar remaining in the bottom of the glass.
Notes
They would have used Stoughton's bitters in 1806, but they don’t make them anymore. Bogart’s, Angostura, or Peychaud’s are all options that would have been around about 20 years after this recipe was written.
Rye whiskey was very popular at the time, so that’s what I used, but the historical recipe isn’t specific, so feel free to use what you like.
To get the same rye whiskey I used, check out the
Drinking History with Max Miller collection at Curiada
.

Potage Crécy (Creamy Carrot and Potato Soup)
Titanic
British Isles
France
20th Century
Oct 15
Written By
Max Miller
Beautifully vibrant carrot and potato soup garnished with homemade croutons and chervil
City/Region:
Carpathia | United Kingdom | France
Time Period:
1903 | 1912
Jump to Recipe
Watch the Episode
While I don’t know if this is the exact soup that was served to the Titanic survivors once they were on board the Carpathia, the captain, Arthur Rostron, ordered for coffee, tea, and soup to be readied for the survivors. The menu from the last meal served aboard the Carpathia before it docked back in New York on April 18th lists Potage Crecy as one of the soups, so if this wasn’t the soup that was first served to survivors, it was at least in the Carpathia’s repertoire.
Dishes featured on the channel rarely make it into my rotation, but this is one of them. It’s simple, quick, and has such a wonderfully rich, buttery, creamy texture and flavor. I was really surprised at how developed the flavors were after such a short cook time, an
potagecrecy.ing:
Ingredients:
Potage
75 g plus 150 g butter*, separated
100 g sliced onion
600 g carrots, thinly sliced in rounds
1 sprig thyme
2 pinches salt
1 pinch sugar
1 L mineral water
250g russet potatoes peeled and chopped into about 1/2-inch cubes
200 ml heavy cream
A few leaves of chervil, parsley, or cilantro, for garnish
Croutons
A handful of about 1/2-inch cubes of French bread
1 to 2 tablespoons butter or better yet, clarified butter or ghee**, for frying
*The butter is a key ingredient in this recipe, so I highly recommend splurging on some high-quality butter. I used a fancy French salted butter.
**Butter will work fine, but clarified butter and ghee have higher
smoke points.
Instructions:
For the soup:
In a large pot over medium-low heat, melt the 75 g of butter. Throughout this recipe, you never want the heat to go above medium, and it’s best to keep it closer to low the whole time.
Once the butter is melted, add the onions, carrots, thyme, salt, and sugar. Stir so that everything gets coated with the butter. Let the butter slowly come to a sizzle. The goal here is to cook the vegetables without letting the onion get any color at all. When the butter is sizzling at the bottom of the pan, place the lid on the pot and cook for 5 minutes. Essentially, you’re just letting the carrots and onions steam.
After 5 minutes, add the mineral water and potatoes and stir. Let it slowly come up to a low simmer, just so you can see a little bubbling, then set the lid back on and cook for another 15 minutes, or until you can mash the potato easily with a fork.
Remove the thyme. To purée the soup, you can either push everything through a strainer, which is in the original recipe but is quite labor intensive, or you can go the modern route and use an immersion blender, which is what I did. Either way, once you have a smooth purée, pass it through a fine sieve to make it even smoother.

pottedmeat.title: Potted Meat — Tasting History
pottedmeat.body:
Watch the Video
For short-term preservation, cooked meat was often potted: pounded to a paste, mixed with spices, packed into a container, and covered with fat. This was kept in a cool place for up to a few weeks, but was often eaten the next day. People potted meat, game, fish, shellfish, cheese, and even mushrooms.
This is really good. It’s essentially roast beef with some spices and butter. What’s not to like? The texture is pȃté-like, but not as smooth, though it spreads easily on some bread.
“
To pot Venison.
Take a piece of venison, fat and lean together, lay it in a dish, and stick pieces of butter all over; tie a brown paper over it, and bake it. When it comes out of the oven, take it out of the liquor hot, drain it, and lay it in a dish; when cold, take off all the skin, and beat it in a marble mortar, fat and lean together, season it with mace, cloves, nutmeg, black pepper and salt to your mind. When the butter is cold that it was baked in, take a little of it, and beat in with it to moisten it; then put it down close, and cover it with clarified butter. You must be sure to beat it, till it is like a paste.
”
— The Art of Cookery, Made Plain and Easy by Hannah Glasse, 1747
pottedmeat.ing:
Ingredients:
3 lbs (1.3 kg) beef bottom round roast, or venison that has some fat in it
1/2 cup (115 g) butter, cut into slices
2 teaspoons salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
1/2 teaspoon nutmeg
1/4 teaspoon mace
1/8 teaspoon cloves
1 cup (225 g) clarified butter* or ghee, melted
See Notes below.
Instructions:
Preheat the oven to 300°F (150°C).
Set the meat in a ceramic baking dish, then cover it with the slices of butter. If your baking dish has a lid, cover it with that. If it doesn’t, then cover it with a piece of parchment paper and secure it with some kitchen twine tied around.
Roast for 3 to 4 hours, or until the meat is 135-140°F (57-60°C). You can use a slow cooker instead; set it on low for 5 to 6 hours.
When the meat is done, take it out of the baking dish and set it aside to cool completely. Pour the drippings through a strainer and save the liquid.
Once the meat is cool, mince it as finely as possible. If you have a food processor, now’s the time to use it.
Working in batches, put the minced meat into a mortar and beat it until it’s as paste-like as you can get it.
Once all the meat has been beaten up, place it in a large bowl and mix in the salt and pepper. Once those are evenly incorporated, mix in the nutmeg, mace, and cloves. Taste and add in more spices if you like.
Add the drippings a little at a time, stirring them in until you get a paste that’s about the texture of tuna salad. I used about 80% of the drippings that I got from my piece of beef.
Pack the beef into jars, crocks, ramekins, or bowls. These were often made of ceramic. Leave about 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) at the top of the jars. You want to pack the beef mixture in tightly so that as little air is in it as possible (air pockets increase the likelihood of spoiling).
Pour the melted clarified butter or ghee over the meat so that it’s covered completely, then put them in the fridge to solidify.
When the clarified butter has solidified, you can leave them as-is or cover them with a lid, piece of parchment

romanmustard.title: Roman Mustard — Tasting History
romanmustard.body:
Watch the Video
Mustard is as old as civilization itself. By 3,000 B.C.E., it was being cultivated in India, and it could be found growing wild from North Africa to the Himalayas. Its leaves, or mustard greens, was used for food, and the seeds were used as medicine. Pliny the Elder in Rome lists the many ailments that mustard seeds were believed to cure, from snake bites to poisonous mushrooms to phlegm to toothaches.
This mustard uses more honey than mustard seeds, and it’s absolutely delicious. You get the flavor of the mustard, but none of the heat. The honey is the dominant flavor, but its sweetness is nicely balanced by the mustard. I would definitely make this again.
“
Take mustard seed in the amount of one and a half sextarii and grind it into a powder. To this add five pounds of honey, one pound of Spanish olive oil, and one sextarius of sharp vinegar. Grind everything together thoroughly, and use.
”
— Palladius’ Opus Agriculturae, late 4th century
romanmustard.ing:
Ingredients:
1/4 cup (50 g) black mustard seeds
1/3 cup (115 g) honey
2 tablespoons olive oil
2 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons wine vinegar, white or red
Instructions:
Grind the mustard seeds in a mortar until it’s the texture you like. A fine powder will make for a smoother mustard.
Stir in the honey until fully incorporated, then stir in the olive oil until it’s fully incorporated, and finally stir in the vinegar until it’s fully incorporated.
The oil and vinegar will separate after a couple of minutes, so be sure to give it another stir before you serve it forth.

sumeriandatecake.title: Sumerian Date Cheesecake — Tasting History
sumeriandatecake.body:
Watch the Video
The inspiration for this recipe comes from a list of ingredients on a cuneiform tablet from the Third Dynasty of Ur around 4,000 years ago. While many historical recipes are vague, this isn’t even pretending to be a recipe. There are a host of unknowns with this cake, including if the cuneiform tablet represents the proportions that were used for the cake, or if this was simply adding on to an existing inventory. We can be pretty sure that flour was also used, but that’s about it. As such, I encourage you to try your own variation and let me know how it turns out in the comments. Your version will be just as correct (or incorrect) as mine, and none of us will get it exactly right.
This cake is very date-heavy and reminds me of steamed British puddings, though it’s much denser and a little dry. If you’re looking to change things up, you might try a salty cheese like feta.
“
gug egala kura
1 sila of butter; 1/3 sila of white cheese; 3 sila first-quality dates; 1/3 sila of Smyrna raisins.
”
— Cuneiform tablet from the Third Dynasty of Ur, c. 2000 B.C.E.
sumeriandatecake.ing:
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups (300 g) pitted dates
3/4 cup (90 g) whole wheat flour
3 tablespoons (45 g) white cheese, I used ricotta, room temperature
1/2 cup (115 g) salted butter, softened
3 tablespoons (30 g) raisins
Grape leaves, jarred or fresh, optional
Instructions:
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Mince the dates, then grind the them in a mortar to make a paste.
In a bowl, combine the flour, cheese, and butter. Work them together with your hands until it’s thoroughly combined.
Add the dates and work them into the dough until evenly distributed. You can add the raisins in now and work them in, or save them to layer below and above the cake. Form the cake into a disc that will fit into your cake pan.
Line the bottom and sides of a round cake pan with either parchment or grape leaves. If you’re using grape leaves, be sure to rinse them well. If you saved the raisins to use now, scatter half of them over the grape leaves, then place the disc of dough on top of them. Scatter the other half over the dough, then cover the top of the dough with parchment or grape leaves. Bake for 30 minutes.
Let the cake cool completely, then unwrap it and serve it forth.

vegetarian

williamshen.title: William the Conqueror’s Hen with Cameline Sauce — Tasting History
williamshen.body:
Watch the Video
The Bayeux Tapestry is an absolutely beautiful piece of embroidery that depicts the military campaign that would make William, Duke of Normandy into William the Conqueror. A good portion of it is dedicated to the first meal William had in England after his men pillaged the surrounding area for food. Here, I’m recreating part of the meal shown there by roasting some Cornish game hens and serving them with Cameline Sauce, a highly spiced and delicious medieval sauce.
We should really go back to larding more things. The guanciale helps keep the game hens incredibly juicy, and while the hens are otherwise unseasoned, the sauce packs enough of a punch to make up for it. It’s a rather thin sauce, but it’s meant for the meat to be dipped in it, not have it poured over the meat. The warm spices are lovely, along with a bit of bite from the vinegar. Since we’re not given measurements for it, feel free to change up the amounts of any of the sauce ingredients to suit your taste.
“
Poules rostis: Roast Pullets.
They should be plucked in water, larded and roasted; they are eaten with Cold Sage Sauce or with Cameline Sauce or with verjus.
To Make Cameline Sauce.
Take ginger, cinnamon in great abundance, cloves, grains of paradise, mace and as much long pepper as you wish; then strain bread that has been soaked in sour wine, and season well with salt.
”
— Le Viandier de Taillevent by Guillaume Tirel, c. 1300
williamshen.ing:
Ingredients:
Hen
1 Cornish game hen
About 1 ounce (30 g) guanciale, cut into small pieces
Cameline Sauce
1 slice white bread, toasted or very stale
1/4 cup (60 ml) red wine
2 tablespoons red wine vinegar
1/2 teaspoon ground ginger
2 teaspoons cinnamon
Pinch ground cloves
Pinch salt
Pinch grains of paradise*
1/4 teaspoon ground mace*
Pinch long pepper*, about 1 piece
*See notes below.
Instructions:
For the hen:
If you’re roasting the hen in the oven, preheat it to 450°F (230°C).
Make shallow cuts all over the Cornish game hen and stick pieces of the guanciale into the cuts. Use more or less guanciale depending on the size of your hen and how much guanciale you want to use.
Tie the legs together with some kitchen twine. If desired, run a large skewer through the bird from end to end. Unless you’re roasting it on a spit of some kind, this is just a decorative nod to the Bayeux Tapestry. If you’re cooking in an oven or barbecue, you don’t need it.
You can now cook the hen however you like. Whichever way you choose, having a pan underneath the hen to catch the drippings is a good idea. To roast yours in the oven like I did, place it in a baking dish, then roast for 20 minutes at 450°F (230°C), then reduce the heat to 350°F (175°C) for another 20 minutes, or until the thickest part of the meat hits 165°F (74°C).
For the cameline sauce:
Remove the crust from the bread and tear it into small pieces. Place these in a bowl and pour the red wine and the vinegar over it. Let it soak for about 10 minutes.
While the bread soaks, grind any of the spices that are whole. Grains of paradise and long pepper often come that way. Mix all of the spices together.
Whisk the spices into the bread and wine. Let this sit for another 5 minutes.
After 5 minutes, taste the sauce and add more of any of the ingredients that you like.
When the sauce is how you like it, pass it through a strainer, pressing on the bread to get all of the liquid out. The sauce will be thinner than what we normally thi

wwiibritishcornedbeefstew.title: WWII British Corned Beef Stew — Tasting History
wwiibritishcornedbeefstew.body:
Watch the Video
The mainstays of rations for British troops in World War II were fairly similar to those of World War I: bully beef and biscuits. Bully beef, or canned corned beef, was often eaten as-is or only slightly warmed up, so this stew, meant to be prepared in large quantities using fresh vegetables, would have been a welcome alternative.
While rather unremarkable and really quite salty, this isn’t half bad. I can certainly see how a hot bowl of this would be nice after days or weeks of cold meals and emergency rations. The texture isn’t my favorite since it’s basically a mush, but if you like canned corned beef, I’d say give this a try.
“
Corned Beef Stew
Preserved meat (12 oz. tins) . .  . . 30 tins
Onions . .  . . 6 lb.
Mixed vegetables . .  . . 4 lb.
Salt and pepper
Stock . .  . . 16 pts.
Dripping . .  . . 1 1/2 lb.
Method
Chop the onions and vegetables and fry-on.
Cut the meat into small cubes.
Put the stock in camp kettle lids or baking dishes and add the rest of the ingredients.
Stir well, bring to the boil and skim; then simmer gently for 1 hour.
”
— Manual of Army Catering Services, 1945
wwiibritishcornedbeefstew.ing:
Ingredients:
3, 12 oz (340 g) cans corned beef
5 tablespoons (70 g) fat*
2 cups (280 g) diced onion
6 1/2 oz (185 g) mixed vegetables**, chopped
1 quart (1 L) beef stock
Pinch of salt
1 teaspoon pepper
*This would have varied depending on what was available. They would have had access to meat drippings, butter, margarine, Crisco, and lard. I used lard.
**This would have also varied. I used a carrot and some potatoes.
Instructions:
Open the cans of corned beef and chop it into small cubes. The size isn’t important as it will all kind of disintegrate later.
Melt the fat in a large pot over high heat. Add the onions and stir to coat them in the fat. Cook for about 5 minutes, or until the onions are translucent and just starting to brown.
Add the vegetables and cook for another 3 minutes or so.
Once the vegetables and onions have browned a bit, add in the corned beef. Give it a stir and cook for 1 minute, then stir in the beef stock, salt, and pepper.
Bring it to a boil, then reduce the heat to a simmer and cover the pot. Simmer for 1 hour. For a full WWII British military ration meal, serve the stew forth with
WWII British Military Ration Scones
.

wwiibritishscones.title: WWII British Military Ration Scones — Tasting History
wwiibritishscones.body:
Watch the Video
The mainstays of rations for British troops in World War II were fairly similar to those of World War I: bully beef and biscuits, or hard tack (clack clack). While military biscuits from World War II aren’t quite as bad as the hard tack of eras gone by, they’re a far cry from delicious. While American Civil War soldiers made their hard tack into dishes like Hell Fired Stew, British WWII soldiers had the option to transform their ration biscuits into scones.
These scones aren’t like the kind you’ll find in a nice bakery or have with afternoon tea, but they are an excellent way to use ration biscuits. They’re flat and dense, but have a wonderful, slightly sweet flavor that reminds me of graham crackers. The recipe says to serve them with jam, so I used some from Wilkin and Sons, who made jam for the British troops’ ration packs during WWII.
“
Scones
Crushed biscuit . . 16 lb.
Dripping . .  . . 4 lb.
Sugar . .  . . 4 lb.
Milk . .  . . 2 tins
Method
Add the sugar to the biscuit.
Rub in the dripping and mix well.
Add sufficient reconstituted milk to make a pliable paste and break into 2-lb. pieces.
Roll out, cut into 4-oz. round scones and place on greased trays.
Bake in a moderate oven for 20 minutes and serve with jam.
”
— Manual of Army Catering Services, 1945
wwiibritishscones.ing:
Ingredients:
1/2 lb (225 g) plain, hard military style biscuits
Heaping 1/2 cup (115 g) sugar
1/2 cup (115 g) fat*, I used butter
1/4 cup (60 ml) evaporated milk
*This would have varied depending on what was available. They would have had access to meat drippings, butter, margarine, Crisco, and lard. I used butter.
Instructions:
Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Break the biscuits into small pieces, then grind them into a fine powder. A blender or food processor is helpful for this, but you can also do it by placing the biscuits in a bowl or zip top bag and crushing them with a rolling pin.
Place the biscuit crumbs in a large bowl, then whisk in the sugar.
Rub the fat into the biscuit crumb mixture until it becomes a sandy texture. Since we’re using biscuit crumbs instead of flour, it won’t behave exactly the same as a regular scone or pie dough, but it should eventually become sandy.
Add about half of the evaporated milk and mix it in. Add more milk little by little until you get a dough that you can roll out.
On a lightly floured surface (they wouldn’t have always had flour, but it’ll make this process much easier), roll the dough out about 1/2 inch (1.5 cm) thick, then cut out scones in 3 inch (8 cm) rounds.
Place the scones on a lined baking sheet and bake for 20 minutes, or until they’re lightly browned.
Let the scones cool, then serve them forth with jam, Wilkin and Sons brand for extra authenticity. For a full WWII British military ration meal, have these scones after a bowl of
WWII British Corned Beef Stew
.

wwiiitaliancarrots.title: WWII Italian Military Carrots — Tasting History
wwiiitaliancarrots.body:
Watch the Video
The state of the Italian military rations during WWII varied widely. At the beginning of the war, Italian troops had a reputation for being exceptionally well fed with 3,500 calories per day that included meat, fat, bread, pasta, heavy stews with fresh vegetables and meat, cakes, sweet pastries, cereal, oatmeal with milk and honey, sliced meats, and copious amounts of cheese. Later on, troops would be glad to get U.S. emergency rations.
This recipe would have been prepared near the beginning of the war when things like lard and fresh vegetables were plentiful, and it’s delicious. The original recipe is for turnips, but the cookbook gives instructions that carrots can be prepared the same way. If turnips aren’t in season, like they weren’t when I made this, the carrots are fantastic.
“
Military-style Turnips
(Quantities for 100 men)
Turnips 15 kg
Lard 500 g
Garlic 50 g
Parsley 500 g
Cheese 200 g
Salt and pepper
At certain times of the year, turnips cost very little, so they can easily be used as a side dish. Peel them and cut them into small pieces or slices. Cook them for 10-15 minutes in salted water. Separately, melt the lard in a pan, add the crushed garlic, and sauté it without letting it brown too much. Remove the garlic and discard it. Add the turnips, well drained of their cooking water, and let them take on the flavor, stirring frequently, for 15-20 minutes. Add the chopped parsley, salt, and pepper. Shortly before serving, add the grated cheese.
”
— Il Cuciniere Militare by Dario Fornari, 1932
wwiiitaliancarrots.ing:
Ingredients:
1.6 lbs (750 g) sliced carrots or turnips, I used orange and purple carrots
2 tablespoons (25 g) lard
1 clove (3 g) crushed garlic
1 cup (25 g) minced parsley
Salt and pepper to taste
Freshly grated parmesan cheese, for topping
Instructions:
Salt a large pot of water, then add the carrots and bring the pot to a boil and boil for 15 minutes, then drain the carrots.
In the same pot, melt the lard. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute, making sure it doesn’t brown too much. Remove the garlic. Add the drained carrots to the pot and stir to coat them in the garlic-flavored lard. Cook, stirring frequently, for 15 minutes.
After 15 minutes, add the parsley and season with salt and pepper to taste. Cook for about 2 more minutes, then serve them forth with plenty of cheese, the
WWII Italian Military Pasta
, and some watered down wine for extra authenticity.

wwiiitalianpasta.title: WWII Italian Military Pasta — Tasting History
wwiiitalianpasta.body:
Watch the Video
Pasta was a staple for the Italian troops at the beginning of WWII, but as the war wore on, food got tighter, but what affected the pasta ration the most was the rationing of water. Desalinated water had a funny taste, which made the pasta taste funny, and at times the water ration was so small that no one was wasting it on cooking pasta.
This recipe would have been made at the beginning of the war, when both food and water were plentiful. It has quite a bit of lard in it, possibly as a way to get more calories to the soldiers, but it is still delicious. The only salt comes from the cooking water for the pasta and the copious amounts of parmesan, but it’s perfect as-is.
“
Military-style pasta
(Sauce quantities for 100 men).
Lard 1.5 kg
Onion 2 kg
Tomato paste 1.5 kg
Pepper 10 g
Cheese 1 kg
Put the lard and onion, well mixed together into a pan. Let them saute, stirring continuously so that the onions brown evenly. Moisten with the tomato paste diluted in about 4 liters of hot water. Add the pepper, let it boil for 20 minutes, and the sauce is ready.
Practical and simple, but certainly inferior to the first two methods described. For variety, this sauce may be made with garlic instead of onion, or with both garlic and onion together, and flavored with 100 g of rosemary. In that case, increase the pepper to 15 g.
”
— Il Cuciniere Militare by Dario Fornari, 1932
wwiiitalianpasta.ing:
Ingredients:
5 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons (75 g) lard or olive oil
1/2 cup (100 g) diced onion
3 cloves (10 g) crushed garlic, optional
4 tablespoons plus 1 teaspoon (75 g) tomato paste
Generous 3/4 cup (200 ml) water
1/2 teaspoon (.75 g) pepper
2 tablespoons (5 g) chopped fresh rosemary, optional
1 lb (450 g) dried pasta, whatever you like
1/2 cup (50 g) freshly grated parmesan cheese
Instructions:
Heat the lard in a wide pan, then add in the onion. This recipe calls for a lot of lard for the amount of onion, so don’t be alarmed if the onions are swimming in it. Let the onions cook, stirring continuously, until they start to brown, about 5 minutes. When the onions have browned, add in the garlic and cook for about 1 minute.
Stir the tomato paste into the water, then add this to the pan along with the pepper. Reduce the heat and let it simmer for 15 minutes.
While the sauce simmers, cook the pasta to your desired doneness.
After the sauce has simmered for 15 minutes, stir in the rosemary and simmer for another 5 minutes.
Toss the cooked pasta in the sauce, then serve it forth with plenty of the cheese, the
WWII Italian Military Carrots
, and some watered down wine for extra authenticity.

main dish
